newsitem.title: zaire: Zaire rebels demand Mobutu's unconditional surrender.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels demand Mobutu's unconditional surrender.

text.p: Frantic efforts to stage top- level negotiations to avert civil war reaching the Zaire capital suffered a setback on Friday when rebels demanded the unconditional surrender of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila hardened his tone over planned face-to-face talks with Mobutu, saying he would only attend a short ceremony on the transfer of power.
Kabila returned on Thursday to Zaire from exploratory talks in South Africa that raised hopes for a negotiated deal to halt six months of civil war.
On Friday he told Reuters by telephone from Zaire's second city Lubumbashi that his forces would march on Kinshasa if Mobutu declined to give up power.
"The South African initiative is about transfer of power. When he is ready for this, I shall go and attend a short day's ceremony on the peaceful transfer of power," he said.
"There will be no protracted negotiations with Mobutu, never, never. Maybe we have been misunderstood. The issue is about transfer of power otherwise we march on to Kinshasa," Kabila added.

But Mobutu's security aide and head of Kinshasa's negotiating team in South Africa, Honore Ngbanda, said Mobutu on Friday accepted President Nelson Mandela's invitation for talks with Kabila which would be held "as soon as possible".
"This morning I gave officially this invitation of President Mandela to President Mobutu and he accepted...but the practical details are being studied," he told reporters.
Ngbanda said the meeting would deal with transitional arrangements, which Mobutu's camp insists must focus on elections to determine if Zaireans want Mobutu or not.

But rebel foreign minister Bizima Karaha, in separate comments on Friday, ruled out any notion of such transitional arrangements by repeating that there would be no truce in the civil war until Mobutu left office without preconditions.

"We don't want any suspension of hostilities. We want the end of the war and that can only come about if the man who brought the war is kicked out. When Mobutu leaves, that will be the end of the war," he told a news conference.

Karaha said talk that pending negotiations would deal with some form of transitional powersharing was incorrect. "What we are negotiating is the mode of departure of Mobutu...The modalities for the end of the dictatorial regime."
Regional military sources told Reuters in Nairobi, Kenya, that Kabila's forces -- already in control of half of Zaire -- appeared to be building up forces for an assault on Kinshasa.
The hardline rebel statements and startling allegations of of a massacre plot stoked anxiety in Kinshasa.
Kabila accused Mobutu through an aide of ordering the massacre of all expatriates in Kinshasa to provoke the intervention of the troops in Congo and avert his downfall.
In a statement to reporters in Lubumbashi Kabila sent the man he wants to be finance minister to give a warning that the alleged plot could "start at any minute".
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga Mobutu, dismissed the allegation as "ridiculous nonsense".
U.S. officials said on Friday they were discounting claims by Zairean rebels that President Mobutu Sese Seko had ordered the massacre of all expatriates in Kinshasa.
"Give it no credence. We're discounting it," he added.

U.S., French, Belgian and British forces based in the nearby Congo capital Brazzaville have stepped up training manoeuvres to prepare for an eventual evacuation of their nationals. About 1,500 Western troops are in Brazzaville.

In a separate development the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it suspended relief work for thousands of Rwandan Hutus in eastern Zaire on Friday after Zaireans attacked its staff in a protest over the presence of the unwanted refugees.

Spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said UNHCR wanted security guarantees from the rebels before resuming aid for more than 80,000 Rwandan Hutus after hundreds of protesters prevented an aid convoy from disembarking from a river ferry on the way to camps.
